analysis.one_liner: Bars the worst practices in high-cost mortgage lending, like balloon payments, financed fees, and forced arbitration.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote in the Senate Banking Committee and died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the rules for high-cost mortgages — loans with above-market rates or heavy fees aimed at borrowers with shaky credit. It would ban balloon payments, limit prepayment penalties, stop lenders from packing single-premium credit insurance into loans, cap the fees that can be financed into the loan balance, require lenders to verify that borrowers can actually afford the payments, and ban forced arbitration. It would also raise fines for violations and extend the time consumers have to sue.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners and buyers with weak credit — the people offered subprime, high-cost mortgages. The bill would cut the hidden charges and loan terms most likely to strip their home equity or put them into foreclosure, and give them stronger legal remedies when lenders break the rules.

how_it_helps.text: Requires lenders to check, using verified income and obligations, whether a borrower can afford the scheduled payments before making a high-cost mortgage — and bans lending based only on the equity in the home [S3].
Prohibits all balloon payments and bans single-premium credit insurance being financed into the loan, two charges that drained equity from subprime borrowers [S3].
Caps what lenders can finance in points and fees and sharply limits prepayment penalties, which had been used to trap borrowers in costly refinancing cycles [S3].
Bans forced arbitration in these loans, raises the civil penalty for violations from $2,000 to $10,000 per violation, and gives consumers three years to sue over violations [S3].

Requires plain-language warnings on the loan itself — that the rate is much higher than most people pay and that the borrower may find a cheaper loan elsewhere — plus a referral to HUD-approved counseling before signing [S3].

analysis.who_pays: High-cost mortgage lenders, mortgage brokers whose compensation would count as fees, and sellers of single-premium credit insurance would lose revenue and face liability. Some borrowers with the weakest credit could find fewer lenders willing to serve them.

drawbacks.text: Lenders would no longer be able to charge the fees, insurance, and penalties the bill targets, and lenders generally would face up to $10,000 per-violation penalties and a longer window for lawsuits [S3].

The mandatory ability-to-repay test and caps on financed fees could make it harder for some borrowers with poor credit histories to get any mortgage at all, since lenders could no longer lend against home equity alone to applicants whose incomes would not cover the payments [S3].

The bill applies only to mortgages that meet its high-cost thresholds, so lenders could restructure loans to stay just under the definitions — the bill directs regulators to write rules against evasion, but enforcement would depend on those rules [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the borrowers these loans target, the protections address the specific practices — equity stripping, credit insurance packing, fee-financing, forced arbitration — that repeatedly led to foreclosure. The honest cost is that some high-risk borrowers might lose access to credit as lenders retreat from restricted products, and that the rules would depend on regulators policing workarounds. On balance the bill's benefits fall on people with the least bargaining power, and its costs on lenders.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late November 2003 and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Paul Sarbanes introduced the bill with 15 Democratic cosponsors on November 21, 2003 [S1].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs — its only committee referral and the only action it ever received [S5].
The Banking Committee never held a markup or sent the bill to the floor, and the full Senate never voted on it before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-cost mortgage lenders and brokers, who faced no new federal restrictions on equity-stripping fees, credit insurance packing, or forced arbitration as the housing boom accelerated.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 15 cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-controlled Banking Committee never acted on the bill; no Republican support appears in the record.

industries.note: The bill targets the core revenue sources of this business: financed points and fees, prepayment penalties, single-premium credit insurance, balloon payments, and loans made without verifying ability to repay. Its profits came from charging borrowers more and from refinancing fees, which runs against the borrowers' interest in keeping their homes.

The bill bans financing single-premium credit life, disability, unemployment, and property insurance into high-cost mortgages, wiping out a major distribution channel for these products, which had added large upfront costs to loans.

All broker compensation would count toward the points-and-fees cap, and only modest fee financing would be allowed, cutting broker income on high-cost loans. Brokers also trigger the bill's stricter rules by originating even a handful of high-cost loans.
Lenders would have to hand borrowers a list of HUD-approved counseling agencies before closing, steering borrowers toward these nonprofit services.
